title: Lists and Tables
description: Choose between ordered and unordered lists based on meaning, build nested lists, and build a genuine table without misusing tables for layout.

objectives.statement: Choose between unordered and ordered lists based on the meaning and order of the content, and build correctly nested list structures.
Identify the purpose of table, tr, th, and td, and build a simple table representing genuine tabular data.
Distinguish tabular data from page layout and explain why tables should not be used as a layout system.

content.title: Lists and Tables
content.hook: In the early 2000s, entire websites were built using tables as an invisible grid to position content. It worked visually, and it broke almost everything else.
content.context: This lesson is about choosing the right element for what content actually is, not what layout you want.
goals: Explain why tables shouldn't be used for layout

content.title: Lists and Tables Represent Real Relationships
content.text: Use an ordered list (<ol>) when the sequence of items actually matters — steps in a recipe, rankings. Use an unordered list (<ul>) when the items form a set with no required order — a list of ingredients, features, or links. Lists can nest: a <li> can contain its own <ul> or <ol> to represent a sub-list. A table (<table>) exists to represent genuinely tabular data — information with real row/column relationships, like a schedule or a price comparison. Inside a table, <tr> marks a row, <th> marks a header cell, and <td> marks an ordinary data cell.

callout.text: If you're using a table because you want two things to sit side by side visually — not because the content has row/column relationships — that's a layout job for CSS, not a job for <table>.

content.keyTakeaway: Choose ul/ol based on whether order matters; choose table only for content that's genuinely tabular.

content.question: You're marking up the steps to assemble a bookshelf, where doing them out of order would break the assembly. Which list type fits?

options.text: It doesn't matter which list type you choose

content.explanation: Because the sequence is meaningful — doing the steps out of order breaks the process — this is a case for an ordered list.

feedback.correct: Right — sequence-dependent steps belong in an ordered list.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — ask whether doing the items in a different order would change the outcome.

content.title: Build a Real Data Table
content.prompt: Build a table listing three programming languages and their release years, with a header row containing 'Language' and 'Year Released'.
content.instructions: Use table, tr, th (for the header row), and td (for the data rows).

testCases.description: Table contains a header row with two th cells
Table contains at least three data rows
Table contains a header row with two th cells
Table contains at least three data rows

feedback.correct: That's a genuine data table with a proper header row.
feedback.incorrect: Check that you have a header row of th cells and at least three td-based data rows.

content.question: Which of these are appropriate uses of an HTML table? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A weekly class schedule with days as columns and time slots as rows
Positioning a logo, a nav menu, and a search box side by side on a page
A price comparison chart across three subscription plans
Arranging three unrelated promotional banners in a row purely for visual layout

content.explanation: A class schedule and a price comparison both have genuine row/column data relationships, which is exactly what tables are for. Positioning unrelated content side by side is a layout task that belongs to CSS, not <table>.

feedback.correct: Right — genuine tabular data belongs in a table; visual positioning doesn't.
feedback.incorrect: Ask which options actually have row/column data relationships versus which are just visual arrangement.

content.title: What You Should Take Away
takeaways: Choose <ol> when sequence matters, <ul> when it doesn't.
Tables exist to represent genuine tabular data via tr/th/td, not to control visual layout.
Using tables for layout is a well-known anti-pattern that breaks accessibility and responsiveness.
